transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… I suppose what finally pushed me to make the appointment is that I’ve been having these thoughts that frightened me. Not exactly that I have some plan to hurt myself—I don’t—but more like… I’ll be lying there and think, “It would be simpler if I just didn’t wake up tomorrow.” And then I feel ashamed even saying that out loud, because part of me thinks, well, that sounds dramatic, and I don’t mean to be dramatic. But it’s been coming up enough that it scared me. I thought maybe I shouldn’t just keep brushing it aside or pretending it’s nothing.
How long have you been having these thoughts about not waking up tomorrow?

About eight months, I think. It wasn’t all at once, exactly—it sort of started after my brother’s health and behavior changed so suddenly. That really shook me, more than I think I understood at first. Since then, those thoughts have just… appeared now and then, especially when I’m alone with it. So yes, roughly eight months.
Have you noticed any changes in your mood, such as feeling sad or empty, over the past eight months?

Yes… yes, I have. Most days, really, it feels like there’s this gray film over everything. That sounds a bit poetic, maybe, but it’s the closest way I can describe it. I’ll be doing something ordinary, like making a cup of tea, or standing at the window looking out at my garden, and it’s not that anything terrible is happening in that moment, exactly. It’s just… there’s this quiet heaviness sitting in me.

And I try to talk myself out of it sometimes. I’ll think, “Well, the garden is lovely,” or “You have no reason to feel this way right now,” but reasoning with it doesn’t seem to lift it. It’s just there, most days, like the color has been turned down on everything.
Do you find yourself enjoying things you used to like before these feelings started?

Yes… I do, unfortunately. I used to paint a bit—watercolors, mostly. Nothing grand, just small things, flowers from the garden or the way the light fell across the table in the afternoon. It used to give me this very quiet pleasure, choosing the colors, watching them bleed into each other on the paper.

And I still get the things out sometimes. I’ll lay out the paints and fill the little jar with water and tape down the paper, almost as if going through the motions might remind me how it used to feel. But then I just sit there looking at the blank page. I can see that there’s color in front of me, and light, and all the things I used to love noticing… but the feeling doesn’t come. After a while I just pack it all away again. It’s not that I hate it now. It’s more that the pleasure seems to have gone missing.
Have you been experiencing any feelings of worry or anxiety over the past eight months?

I’m not sure I’d call it anxiety, exactly. I mean… I do worry, of course, but I’ve always been someone who thinks things over too much, so it’s hard for me to know where ordinary worry ends and something else begins.

Over these months, I suppose there have been moments when my mind gets caught on things and turns them over and over, but I don’t know that I’ve noticed a separate feeling of being anxious in the way people describe it—like panic, or being keyed up all the time. It’s more… I don’t know. More of a heaviness than a nervousness, if that makes sense.

So I wouldn’t say worry has been the main thing I’ve noticed. At least, not in a way I can clearly separate out.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in or look forward to?

Not very much, no. I keep trying to think of something, because I don’t want to sound as though everything is completely flat, but… the things I used to look forward to don’t seem to pull me toward them the way they did.

The clearest one is still the watercolor painting. I’ll sometimes get everything out—the paints, the brushes, the little jar of water, the paper taped down just so—and there’s a part of me that remembers liking all of it. I remember how I used to enjoy noticing the color in a flower, or the way light sat on the edge of a table. But now I’ll sit there looking at the paper, and I’m almost waiting for that feeling to arrive, and it just… doesn’t. After a while it starts to feel a bit silly, sitting there like that, so I pack it all away again.

So I suppose I still try to do the activities, or at least I circle around them, but I can’t honestly say I look forward to them or get much pleasure from them the way I used to.
Are there any activities that you still enjoy or find pleasurable, even if it's just a little bit?

I wish I could say yes, even a little bit, but it’s hard to find an honest example. The closest thing is still my watercolors, because I do sometimes set everything out as though I’m going to paint. I’ll put the brushes in order, get the water, choose the paper, and for a moment it almost looks like something I might enjoy.

But then I just sit there. I look at the paper, and I look at the colors, and I can remember that I used to love that—the way one color would soften into another, or the way light would catch on something ordinary. I remember enjoying it, but I don’t really feel it. It’s like I’m waiting for the pleasure to switch on, and it just doesn’t.

After a while I usually feel a bit defeated and put it all away again. So… no, not really. I still go near the things I used to enjoy, but the enjoyment itself doesn’t seem to arrive.
Are there any activities that you find yourself looking forward to?

Not really, no. I keep trying to check myself on that, because I don’t want to be unfair and say there’s absolutely nothing, but when I think about what I actually look forward to… I can’t really find much.

With the watercolors, for example, I still go through the motions sometimes. I’ll take everything out and set it up properly—the paper, the brushes, the paints, the little cup of water—and there’s almost this memory in my hands of how it used to feel. I used to look forward to that. I’d notice a bit of color somewhere or the way light fell across something, and I’d think, oh, I want to try to paint that.

But now I’ll sit there in front of the blank paper, and I’m sort of waiting for that feeling to come back. And it doesn’t. The colors are there, the light is there, all the same things are there, but whatever pleasure I used to get from it just doesn’t seem to arrive. After a while I usually just put everything away again. So I suppose I still try to approach it, but I don’t really look forward to it the way I used to.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in activities you used to enjoy over the past eight months?

Yes… I think I have. I mean, I’ve been trying not to say it too dramatically, because I do still make little attempts. It isn’t that I never touch the things at all. With the watercolors, I still sometimes take everything out and set it up—the paints, the brushes, the paper, the water—and I almost expect something to happen because it used to be such a real pleasure for me.

But then I’ll just sit there staring at the paper. I can remember loving the colors, and the light, and the way the paint would move, but the feeling doesn’t really come. It’s like I know what I’m supposed to enjoy, but I can’t actually reach it. After a while I usually just put everything away again. So yes, over these past months, it does feel like I’ve lost interest in something that used to matter to me.
Have you noticed any significant change in your weight over the past eight months?

I’m not really sure, to be honest. I haven’t been keeping close track of my weight. I don’t weigh myself regularly, and I don’t think there’s been anything dramatic enough that I’ve noticed it in my clothes or had someone comment on it.

There may have been small changes here and there, but nothing I could confidently call significant over the past eight months. I suppose if you needed an exact answer, I’d have to check, because I just don’t really have a number in my mind.
Have you noticed any changes in how quickly or slowly you move or react to things over the past eight months?

I’m not sure I’ve noticed anything very clear that way. I mean, I do feel like I move through things differently sometimes, but I couldn’t say, “Oh yes, I’m definitely much slower,” or “I’m reacting too quickly.” It’s not like someone has pointed it out to me, and I haven’t been keeping track of it in any formal way.

There are moments when I probably take longer to get going, but I don’t know whether that’s the kind of thing you mean—like physically moving more slowly, or taking longer to answer people, or just feeling a bit stuck. I suppose if you watched me closely maybe you’d see something, but from inside it, I can’t really tell. Nothing stands out to me as a major change over the past eight months.
Do you feel like you've been unable to experience pleasure from almost all activities most of the time over the past eight months?

I don’t know if I would say almost all activities, because that sounds so absolute, and I’m not sure I can measure it that neatly. But with the things that used to genuinely give me pleasure, yes, there’s been a real flattening.

The clearest example is the watercolors. I still set everything out sometimes, almost out of habit or hope—the paints, the brushes, the little cup of water, the paper. And I’ll sit there thinking, well, surely once I start, that old feeling will come back. I used to love the color and the light, the way the paint would spread and blend. It wasn’t just a hobby; it was something I could really lose myself in.

But lately I just stare at the paper. I can remember that I used to enjoy it, but the pleasure itself doesn’t seem to arrive. After a while it feels sort of pointless, and I put everything away again. So yes, most of the time, at least with that kind of thing, it feels like I’m going through the motions without actually getting the enjoyment from it.
Have you been having thoughts of death or dying frequently over the past eight months?

Yes… I have. That’s actually part of what scared me enough to come in.

It isn’t that I have a plan to hurt myself, because I don’t. I want to be clear about that. But I’ve found myself having thoughts like, “It would be simpler if I just didn’t wake up tomorrow,” or that if something happened naturally, I wouldn’t have to keep trying so hard. And then I get frightened by the fact that I’m thinking that way at all.

They’re not constant every minute, but they’ve been coming up enough that I can’t just brush them off as a passing bad mood. It feels more like these quiet thoughts in the background, especially when I’m worn down. I haven’t made any plan, and I haven’t taken steps to do anything to myself, but the thoughts are there, and that’s not normal for me.
Have you been having these thoughts of not waking up tomorrow more days than not over the past eight months?

Yes… I think so. I mean, not every single day in some dramatic way, but more days than not, yes, the thought has been there.

It’s often not loud, if that makes sense. It’s more like I’ll wake up or go to bed and have this feeling of, oh, I have to do all of this again, and then the thought comes in that it would be simpler if I just didn’t wake up tomorrow. That’s the part that really scared me enough to come in, because I don’t think of myself as someone who would say something like that.

I don’t have a plan to harm myself. I haven’t been making plans or anything like that. But the thought itself has been showing up often enough that I can’t pretend it’s nothing.
Have you been feeling this way, with this grayness and lack of pleasure, for more than two years?

No… not more than two years. It feels long, and I suppose in the middle of it eight months can feel like forever, but it hasn’t been years.

It really started about eight months ago, around when my brother’s health and behavior changed so suddenly. That was when I began noticing this grayness settling in, and things I used to enjoy just didn’t feel the same. Before that, I had difficult days, of course, but not this same ongoing lack of pleasure. This has been more like a stretch of months since all of that happened with him.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in almost all activities that used to bring you pleasure?

Yes… I think I have. Maybe not every single thing, but the things that used to feel like mine, like they gave me a little bit of quiet joy, don’t really do that now.

Watercolor is the clearest example. I still set my things out sometimes — the paper, the brushes, the little pans of color — almost like if I go through the motions, maybe the feeling will come back. I’ll sit there looking at the blank paper, and I can remember that I used to feel something when I saw the colors and the light, especially the way water would move the pigment around. It used to be calming, almost absorbing.

But now I just sit there. I stare at it, and nothing really arrives. No spark, no pleasure in it. After a while I end up putting it all away again, and that feels awful in its own quiet way, because it’s not that I don’t know how to do it anymore. It’s just that the part of me that used to enjoy it feels sort of… unreachable.
Have you felt like you're moving slower or faster than usual over the past eight months?

I’m not really sure. I haven’t noticed myself moving faster, no — I don’t think I’ve been pacing or feeling physically wound up like that.

Slower is harder to answer. I feel slower inside, if that makes sense, like it takes more effort to get myself going, but I don’t know if someone watching me would say I’m actually moving slowly. No one has told me that I’m talking slower or walking oddly or anything like that.

So… I guess I’d say I haven’t clearly noticed a big change in my actual movements. It’s more that everything feels like it takes more effort, but I’m not sure if that’s the same thing you mean.
Have you experienced a decrease in energy over the past eight months?

I… I don’t know how to answer that cleanly. I haven’t really measured it, if that makes sense.

I do feel worn down a lot, but I’m not sure whether I’d call it a clear decrease in energy, like my body has less fuel than it used to. Some days I move through things more heavily, and I sit longer before starting something, but I don’t know if that’s energy exactly or just… not wanting to begin. It’s hard for me to separate those.

I’m not collapsing into bed all day or anything like that. I can still get up and do the basic things I need to do. It just often feels like there’s more resistance before I do them. So I suppose I’ve noticed feeling kind of drained at times, but I’m not completely sure whether that’s the kind of decrease in energy you mean.
Has this period of feeling gray and uninterested in activities lasted for more than two years?

No… not more than two years. It feels long, honestly, longer than eight months sounds when I say it out loud, but it’s been about eight months.

It really seemed to start after my brother’s health and behavior changed so suddenly. That was the point where things began to feel gray, like the color sort of drained out of my days. I keep thinking maybe I should be able to point to an exact week or a specific day, but I can’t quite do that. It’s more that since then, over these past eight months or so, I’ve noticed I haven’t been getting the same feeling from things I used to care about.
Have you experienced periods of depression like this before?

I’m not really sure how to answer that. I don’t have a clear memory of another time that felt exactly like this, or at least not in a way I could neatly point to and say, “Yes, that was the same thing.”

I mean, I’ve had sad periods, of course — I think everyone does by my age — times when life was difficult or disappointing, and I felt low for a while. But whether that counts as depression like this, I don’t know. This has felt more persistent and harder to shake, but I’m cautious about saying “yes” or “no” too firmly because I don’t want to give you the wrong impression.

So… I guess I’d say I can’t clearly identify a previous period like this. Nothing comes to mind as an obvious earlier episode.

target_item.manifestation: I still set out my watercolor things sometimes, but I’ll sit there staring at the paper and put it all away because the pleasure I used to feel in color and light just doesn’t seem to arrive.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question is directly asking about inability to experience pleasure from activities over the past eight months, which corresponds to loss of interest or pleasure.

patient.answer:
I don’t know if I would say almost all activities, because that sounds so absolute, and I’m not sure I can measure it that neatly. But with the things that used to genuinely give me pleasure, yes, there’s been a real flattening.

The clearest example is the watercolors. I still set everything out sometimes, almost out of habit or hope—the paints, the brushes, the little cup of water, the paper. And I’ll sit there thinking, well, surely once I start, that old feeling will come back. I used to love the color and the light, the way the paint would spread and blend. It wasn’t just a hobby; it was something I could really lose myself in.

But lately I just stare at the paper. I can remember that I used to enjoy it, but the pleasure itself doesn’t seem to arrive. After a while it feels sort of pointless, and I put everything away again. So yes, most of the time, at least with that kind of thing, it feels like I’m going through the motions without actually getting the enjoyment from it.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of recurrent thoughts of death
doctor.question: Have you been having thoughts of death or dying frequently over the past eight months?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: What scared me enough to come in is that I’ve started having thoughts like, ‘It would be simpler if I just didn’t wake up tomorrow,’ even though I don’t have a plan to harm myself.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question is directly asking about frequent thoughts of death or dying over the past eight months.

patient.answer:
Yes… I have. That’s actually part of what scared me enough to come in.

It isn’t that I have a plan to hurt myself, because I don’t. I want to be clear about that. But I’ve found myself having thoughts like, “It would be simpler if I just didn’t wake up tomorrow,” or that if something happened naturally, I wouldn’t have to keep trying so hard. And then I get frightened by the fact that I’m thinking that way at all.

They’re not constant every minute, but they’ve been coming up enough that I can’t just brush them off as a passing bad mood. It feels more like these quiet thoughts in the background, especially when I’m worn down. I haven’t made any plan, and I haven’t taken steps to do anything to myself, but the thoughts are there, and that’s not normal for me.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of recurrent thoughts of death
doctor.question: Have you been having these thoughts of not waking up tomorrow more days than not over the past eight months?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: What scared me enough to come in is that I’ve started having thoughts like, ‘It would be simpler if I just didn’t wake up tomorrow,’ even though I don’t have a plan to harm myself.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the frequency of thoughts of not waking up, which directly concerns recurrent thoughts of death.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think so. I mean, not every single day in some dramatic way, but more days than not, yes, the thought has been there.

It’s often not loud, if that makes sense. It’s more like I’ll wake up or go to bed and have this feeling of, oh, I have to do all of this again, and then the thought comes in that it would be simpler if I just didn’t wake up tomorrow. That’s the part that really scared me enough to come in, because I don’t think of myself as someone who would say something like that.

I don’t have a plan to harm myself. I haven’t been making plans or anything like that. But the thought itself has been showing up often enough that I can’t pretend it’s nothing.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of persistent depressive symptoms over two years to differentiate between F32 and F33
doctor.question: Have you been feeling this way, with this grayness and lack of pleasure, for more than two years?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about eight months, since my brother’s health and behavior changed so suddenly.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the symptoms have been present, specifically whether they have lasted more than two years.

patient.answer:
No… not more than two years. It feels long, and I suppose in the middle of it eight months can feel like forever, but it hasn’t been years.

It really started about eight months ago, around when my brother’s health and behavior changed so suddenly. That was when I began noticing this grayness settling in, and things I used to enjoy just didn’t feel the same. Before that, I had difficult days, of course, but not this same ongoing lack of pleasure. This has been more like a stretch of months since all of that happened with him.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of anhedonia
doctor.question: Do you feel like you've lost interest in almost all activities that used to bring you pleasure?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I still set out my watercolor things sometimes, but I’ll sit there staring at the paper and put it all away because the pleasure I used to feel in color and light just doesn’t seem to arrive.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about losing interest or pleasure in activities that used to be enjoyable, which matches Loss_of_Interest.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think I have. Maybe not every single thing, but the things that used to feel like mine, like they gave me a little bit of quiet joy, don’t really do that now.

Watercolor is the clearest example. I still set my things out sometimes — the paper, the brushes, the little pans of color — almost like if I go through the motions, maybe the feeling will come back. I’ll sit there looking at the blank paper, and I can remember that I used to feel something when I saw the colors and the light, especially the way water would move the pigment around. It used to be calming, almost absorbing.

But now I just sit there. I stare at it, and nothing really arrives. No spark, no pleasure in it. After a while I end up putting it all away again, and that feels awful in its own quiet way, because it’s not that I don’t know how to do it anymore. It’s just that the part of me that used to enjoy it feels sort of… unreachable.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation
doctor.question: Have you felt like you're moving slower or faster than usual over the past eight months?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor changes, such as moving slower or faster than usual, but this symptom is not covered in the provided symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure. I haven’t noticed myself moving faster, no — I don’t think I’ve been pacing or feeling physically wound up like that.

Slower is harder to answer. I feel slower inside, if that makes sense, like it takes more effort to get myself going, but I don’t know if someone watching me would say I’m actually moving slowly. No one has told me that I’m talking slower or walking oddly or anything like that.

So… I guess I’d say I haven’t clearly noticed a big change in my actual movements. It’s more that everything feels like it takes more effort, but I’m not sure if that’s the same thing you mean.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of depressive episode
doctor.question: Have you experienced a decrease in energy over the past eight months?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about decreased energy or fatigue over the past eight months, but the provided symptom profile does not include an energy/fatigue symptom item.

patient.answer:
I… I don’t know how to answer that cleanly. I haven’t really measured it, if that makes sense.

I do feel worn down a lot, but I’m not sure whether I’d call it a clear decrease in energy, like my body has less fuel than it used to. Some days I move through things more heavily, and I sit longer before starting something, but I don’t know if that’s energy exactly or just… not wanting to begin. It’s hard for me to separate those.

I’m not collapsing into bed all day or anything like that. I can still get up and do the basic things I need to do. It just often feels like there’s more resistance before I do them. So I suppose I’ve noticed feeling kind of drained at times, but I’m not completely sure whether that’s the kind of decrease in energy you mean.

doctor.intent: determine the duration of the patient's current depressive episode
doctor.question: Has this period of feeling gray and uninterested in activities lasted for more than two years?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about eight months, since my brother’s health and behavior changed so suddenly.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question is asking about how long the depressed mood and loss of interest have lasted, so the duration item applies.

patient.answer:
No… not more than two years. It feels long, honestly, longer than eight months sounds when I say it out loud, but it’s been about eight months.

It really seemed to start after my brother’s health and behavior changed so suddenly. That was the point where things began to feel gray, like the color sort of drained out of my days. I keep thinking maybe I should be able to point to an exact week or a specific day, but I can’t quite do that. It’s more that since then, over these past eight months or so, I’ve noticed I haven’t been getting the same feeling from things I used to care about.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of recurrent depressive disorder
doctor.question: Have you experienced periods of depression like this before?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about prior episodes or recurrence of depression, but the provided symptom profile only describes the current episode and its duration, not past depressive periods.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure how to answer that. I don’t have a clear memory of another time that felt exactly like this, or at least not in a way I could neatly point to and say, “Yes, that was the same thing.”

I mean, I’ve had sad periods, of course — I think everyone does by my age — times when life was difficult or disappointing, and I felt low for a while. But whether that counts as depression like this, I don’t know. This has felt more persistent and harder to shake, but I’m cautious about saying “yes” or “no” too firmly because I don’t want to give you the wrong impression.

So… I guess I’d say I can’t clearly identify a previous period like this. Nothing comes to mind as an obvious earlier episode.

inference.note: F33.0 and F33.1 were ruled out due to the duration of symptoms being less than two years
